lessons.title: The legal framework for employment
lessons.html:
The legal framework for employment

A poultry farm manager is responsible for staff who work shifts, weekends and public holidays, because birds need care every day. Personnel management must therefore balance continuous operations with legal obligations and fair treatment.

Core legislation

  • Constitution: the Bill of Rights includes fair labour practices and the right to join trade unions.
  • Labour Relations Act: fair dismissal, disciplinary and grievance processes, collective bargaining, unfair labour practices, the CCMA and bargaining councils.
  • Basic Conditions of Employment Act: working hours, overtime, Sunday and public holiday work, night work, leave, notice, payslips.
  • National Minimum Wage Act and sector rules for farm workers: minimum pay.
  • Employment Equity Act: no unfair discrimination; affirmative action plans for designated employers.
  • Skills Development Act and Skills Development Levies Act: training, workplace skills plans, AgriSETA.
  • Unemployment Insurance Act: UIF registration and contributions.
  • OHS Act 85 of 1993 and the Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act: safety and injury compensation.
  • Protection of Personal Information Act: lawful handling of employee personal information.

Laws and minimum wages change; managers must check current requirements with HR, labour consultants or the Department of Employment and Labour.

Shift work

Poultry operations need rosters covering early mornings, weekends and holidays. Rosters must comply with daily and weekly hour limits, rest periods and premium pay rules. Publish rosters in advance and rotate weekend duty fairly.

Employment contracts

Every employee must receive written particulars of employment. Fixed-term and seasonal contracts must be clearly worded. Policies such as the disciplinary code, biosecurity rules and leave procedures should be explained and acknowledged.

lessons.title: Human resource planning, recruitment and development
lessons.html:
Human resource planning, recruitment and development

Workforce planning

Work out how many people with which skills are needed per house, per shift and per function (production, egg room, maintenance, cleaning crews, security). Consider peak periods such as placement, depletion and clean-out. Plan for absenteeism, leave and turnover so that bird care is never compromised.

Job descriptions

Write job descriptions for each role: purpose, main duties, required skills, reporting lines, working conditions (including biosecurity restrictions such as not keeping birds at home, if that is farm policy). Clear job descriptions support recruitment, training and performance management.

Recruitment and selection

  1. Define the requirements from the job description.
  2. Advertise fairly, internally and externally.
  3. Shortlist against the criteria.
  4. Interview with structured questions; use practical tests where suitable.
  5. Check references and documents.
  6. Make the offer in writing.

Avoid unfair discrimination at every step. Keep records of the process.

Induction

Induction should cover the farm, rules, biosecurity, health and safety, animal welfare, the employee's role and house routines, pay and leave, and who to go to with problems. Biosecurity induction is critical: one careless new worker can bring disease onto the farm.

Training and development

Identify training needs from job requirements, performance reviews and new technology. Combine on-the-job training with formal courses, learnerships and skills programmes through AgriSETA-accredited providers. Prepare a workplace skills plan if required, and claim applicable grants. Develop promising staff into team leader and supervisor roles to build internal capacity.

Retention

Turnover is costly: recruitment, training and lost productivity. Fair pay, good working conditions, respectful supervision, development opportunities and recognition all improve retention.

lessons.title: Performance, discipline and employee relations
lessons.html:
Performance, discipline and employee relations

Performance management

Set clear expectations and measures for each role - for example mortality, weight targets and record accuracy for house workers; packing accuracy and breakages for egg room staff. Give regular feedback, coach, and hold formal reviews. Link development and recognition to performance.

Incapacity: poor performance and ill health

When an employee cannot meet standards, the employer must follow a fair process: inform the employee of the shortfall, provide training, support and a reasonable time to improve, and consider alternatives before dismissal. Ill health or injury requires investigation of the extent of incapacity and reasonable accommodation where possible.

Misconduct and discipline

A disciplinary code sets rules and typical sanctions. Discipline must be substantively fair (a valid rule, known to the employee, consistently applied, appropriate sanction) and procedurally fair (investigation, notice of allegations, opportunity to respond with representation, impartial decision, right to appeal where the code provides). Serious biosecurity breaches, theft, assault, and working under the influence may be serious offences under the farm's code. Progressive discipline - counselling, verbal warning, written warning, final written warning - is used for less serious, repeated offences.

Grievances

A grievance procedure allows employees to raise complaints without fear. Handle grievances promptly, at the lowest appropriate level, with escalation steps and records.

Employee relations

Respect employees' rights to join unions and to engage through recognised structures. Communicate openly about changes such as new rosters, technology or restructuring, and consult where the law requires. Retrenchments must follow the consultation procedures of the Labour Relations Act.

Wellbeing

Provide clean facilities, safe working conditions and protective equipment. Address issues such as fatigue from shift work, exposure to dust and ammonia, and stress during disease outbreaks or mass culling, which can be distressing for staff.

Key points

  • Personnel management on poultry farms must cover continuous, shift-based work legally.
  • Use job descriptions, fair recruitment and thorough biosecurity induction.
  • Plan training through workplace skills plans and AgriSETA programmes.
  • Handle incapacity and misconduct with substantive and procedural fairness.
  • Support wellbeing, especially during disease outbreaks and culling.
